title: FSSAI Puts Influencers and Celebrities on Notice Over Misleading Food Promotions
excerpt: India's food safety regulator is tightening the screws on celebrity endorsements and influencer marketing in the food and beverage sector, backed by new enforcement tools and a parliamentary push for stricter labelling rules.
body:
• FSSAI has issued notices to multiple food companies over misleading claims like "100% Natural" and "energy drinks," forcing relabelling across the industry
  • Celebrity food endorsements account for 28% of all celebrity-endorsed ads in India, according to TAM AdEx data
  • The regulator filed an FIR against social media influencers for allegedly circulating misleading content about FSSAI itself
  • A parliamentary committee has recommended stricter front-of-pack labelling with colour-coded warnings and graded penalties for repeat violations
  • India's health food market, valued at $25.8 billion, is projected to reach $59.8 billion by 2034

A Regulatory Reckoning for Food Marketing

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is escalating its crackdown on misleading food promotions, targeting not just brands but the celebrities and influencers who endorse them. The regulatory push comes as India's health food market surges past $25.8 billion and is projected to hit $59.8 billion by 2034, according to market research firm Imarc.

In recent months, FSSAI has issued notices to a string of companies over dubious labelling claims. MasterChow Foods was questioned over claims like "100% Natural" and "Freshly Made." Emami Healthy & Tasty received a notice for what FSSAI called its "misleading" nomenclature. Six beverage companies, including Sting Energy and Hell Energy, were hauled up for using the term "energy drinks." PepsiCo has already begun removing the word "energy" from new cans and bottles of Sting, according to Forbes India.

"A food label is no longer just packaging. It's becoming a scientific and legal document."

— Ashwin Bhadri, Founder and CEO, Equinox Labs

The Celebrity Endorsement Problem

Celebrity food endorsements sit at the centre of the controversy. The 2024 TAM AdEx report found that food and beverage advertisements accounted for 28 percent of all celebrity-endorsed ads in India. While the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 prohibits celebrities from endorsing banned products, it still allows promotions of legal products unless explicitly prohibited by law.

ASCI CEO Manisha Kapoor has noted that influencers frequently promote foods without disclosing financial ties to brands, making endorsements appear organic rather than paid sponsorships. "The continuous exposure to such ads makes it difficult for consumers to make informed choices," said Sweta Rajan, a partner at Economic Laws Practice, according to Storyboard18.

The Department of Consumer Affairs has introduced supplementary guidelines requiring celebrities, influencers, and even virtual influencers to provide clear disclaimers when sharing health-related information or endorsing food products. Endorsements must now use terms like "advertisement," "sponsored," or "paid promotion," and individuals cannot endorse products they have not personally used.

FSSAI Takes Legal Action Against Influencers

In a separate but related move, FSSAI filed an FIR against several social media influencers in April, alleging a coordinated campaign to damage its reputation through misleading online content. Delhi Police registered the case under Section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (criminal breach of trust) and Section 72 of the IT Act (breach of confidentiality), according to FoodTech Network.

The regulator alleged that some influencer accounts circulated confidential FSSAI documents that may have been accessed without authorisation and tampered with before being shared. The move drew mixed reactions, with critics calling it an overreach against free speech.

Parliament Pushes for Tougher Rules

A parliamentary committee has added its weight to the enforcement push. In a July 2026 report, the committee recommended that FSSAI finalise its long-delayed front-of-pack nutrition labelling regulations, which were issued in draft form in September 2022. The committee called for colour-coded warnings on products high in sugar, graded penalties for repeat violations, and mandatory timelines for withdrawing non-compliant advertisements, according to The Hindu Business Line.

The committee also urged stronger coordination between the Department of Consumer Affairs and FSSAI through structured information-sharing mechanisms and joint review meetings.

Industry Scrambles to Comply

For food companies, the regulatory shift is forcing operational overhauls. Relabelling alone involves redesigning artwork, obtaining fresh regulatory approvals, replacing packaging material, and coordinating changes across supply chains. "For businesses with hundreds of stock keeping units, even a small word change can become an operational exercise," said Bhadri of Equinox Labs.

Health food brand The Whole Truth recently replaced its "no added sugar" claim with "sweetened with dates" on its chocolate packaging. Organic Wisdom received a notice for misleading consumers about the organic status of its products without mandatory certifications.

"Consumers are becoming more informed and are increasingly valuing transparency over marketing hype."

— Sahil Kukreja, Co-founder, The Func Lab

The regulatory landscape has shifted from treating labelling norms as advisory to enforcing them with teeth. As FSSAI deploys digital tools like its Food Safety Compliance System and electronic Product and Claim Approval Application System to track violations at scale, the days of vague health claims and undisclosed celebrity endorsements in India's food sector appear numbered.
